svg.text: Arterial blood pressure over the cardiac cycle
mm Hg
systolic 120
ventricular systole: pressure rises sharply
diastolic 75-85
ventricles relax: lowest pressure before the next beat
written as 120/80; measured with a sphygmomanometer
(a rising and falling mercury column); highest in the aorta,
falling along the systemic arteries; the pulse is the
throbbing of the elastic artery walls
Regulation of blood pressure
Short term: baroreceptors (nervous)
pressure receptors in the carotid arteries and the aortic
arch; when pressure falls they signal the brain, which
raises the rate and force of the heartbeat and constricts
the arterioles until pressure is normal again
Long term: hormones and blood volume
low volume and pressure: brain receptors cause thirst and
make the posterior pituitary release ADH, so the kidneys
keep more water and the arterioles constrict: pressure rises
high volume stretches the right atrium, whose endocrine
cells release ANH; more salt and water leave in the urine,
so volume and pressure fall
Hypertension
chronic pressure above 140/90 from faulty nervous or hormonal
control, stress, obesity, high salt, smoking or heredity;
risks vessel rupture (brain haemorrhage), weakens the heart
(congestive heart failure) and damages the nephrons
Blood pressure is the force of the blood on the inner walls of the vessels; the term usually means systemic arterial pressure.
